utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, Alex Demirdjian, with Tom Hannis, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Claire Plumb appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin, the -- we remind -- we note that the Defence had been asked for expedited responses in respect of a motion to add six documents in respect of a witness, and those -- such responses not being forthcoming, unless there is some response from the Defence, the -- the Chamber will proceed on the basis that no such responses would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I'm not able to give my comments because I will have to consult with the -- with Mr. O'Sullivan about that particular motion. And if I can give the -- our response by -- by -- after the first session. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to confirm there is a submitted joint response today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect to the application by the Prosecution in the 17th motion for protective measures filed on the 29th of October, 2010, the Chamber grants the motion as prayed in respect of Witnesses 48, 88, 145, 153, and -- and denies the motion, without prejudice, in respect of Witnesses 32 and 36. Are there any other procedural or housekeeping matters before we call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There's a couple of matters relating to the very next witness. But prior to that, I'll leave to Ms. Pidwell to deal with some scheduling matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just to follow up from your rulings yesterday in relation to the scheduling matters. Firstly, I can advise that the witness that Your Honours kindly acceded to our request to add him on to the videolink for next week that's already in place, when we went back to the witness, he has recovered from his influenza or whatever it was that was causing him problems and has now confirmed he is able to travel. So he will be here live next week. So I've -- we've already notified the Defence and the Registry, but we'll put that on the record for Your Honours. The second matter is in relation to Witness 228 who you ruled on yesterday. I would ask for your indulgence to hear me on this matter to reconsider your ruling to bring him in, in December. With the greatest respect to Ms. Korner, she didn't provide you with the complete picture of this witness's individual circumstances and the reasons why we are wanting to coordinate his testimony with that of another trial. And if I may ask to go into private session, I'm able to provide you with some further details on that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do we already have a submission on that call-back, or were you still considering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I orally -- officially asked in the transcript, orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You already -- so it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's with us then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just one additional factor in respect of that. If the witness is required -- that witness is required to attend, he was, from my recollection, a subpoenaed witness the last time he attended. And, accordingly, we would need some time to make those arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would consider this in the course of -- of the day and get back to the parties. Is there anything else before the witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, it's in relation to the witness itself, Your Honours. Two brief matters, I hope. First of all, when I met with the witness yesterday, he indicated for the first time that he wanted some protective measures. Could we shortly go into private session just so that I can deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the second topic, Your Honours, it's in relation to the time we have this morning with this witness. In your oral decision on the 11th of November, 2010, you granted us 30 minutes to call him as a viva voce witness. And you ordered that the examination be limited to the facts pertaining to the enforcement of the curfew. As you'll remember, we have conflicting evidence in relation to the enforcement of the curfew in the municipality of Doboj. Now, having had the benefit of meeting the witness yesterday, I would like to alert Your Honours that there are a number of topics that he can deal with in support of his evidence relating to the curfew. He was, like I said, of some leadership position at the time, and he can give you a lot of background information to support what he is going to say in relation to the curfew. As I have mentioned to you earlier, he knew members of the Crisis Staff, and that will give you the basis upon which he is giving this evidence. Additionally, as I indicated in the e-mail, the slow pace with which the witness provides his answers might be difficult to complete his evidence in 30 minutes. If I can put it this way: Interpreters will have no problems following him. So 30 minutes will be a little, just a little, too tight. An additional thing that you may want to consider is that -- in relation to the next witness who is starting right after him, I have indications from Mr. Rindi that he may less time than the one hour that he's been granted, so we may even be in a position to finish both witnesses today. I'm not going to take more time than needed on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So how much more than the 30 minutes are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: An additional 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Demirdjian, we stay within the limits of the curfew, even if you go a little bit beyond contextual-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We are focussing absolutely on the curfew. I will have to deal with his background - who he was and what position he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- who did he deal with, but we're sticking with the curfew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we should go into closed session for the examination and further re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I would just deliver the Chamber's Ruling on the protective measures in public, and the Ruling is that the Chamber has granted that protective measures of a pseudonym and face distortion for this witness, who, throughout these proceedings, will be referred to as ST-041. And the second thing I would like to do before I give the floor to the Prosecution is to ask the Registrar to assign an exhibit number to the pseudonym sheet that was signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The pseudonym sheet for Witness ST-041 shall be given Exhibit P01728, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I start, I would like to remind you that it is not a sign of disrespect, but I will referring to you as "Witness" or as your pseudonym, "ST-041." You already indicated to Their Honours your religion, your name, and your date of birth. I would like to ask you, first of all, about the military service. Did you complete your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and which year was that in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1966 and 1967. In Nis and in Vranje, in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You also indicated your position to the Judges. I will not be referring to it; however, is it correct to say that within the organisation you were working in, you were a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when did you start working for that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when did you stop working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how it came that the 30th of April was the last day of your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The 30th of April, 1992, was the last working day in the month of April, before a holiday that's celebrated there, and that's the 1st of May. The next day was a public holiday, so we did not work. And the 2nd of May was also a public holiday. And between the night of the 2nd and the 3rd of May, Doboj was taken over by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, how did it come that you stopped working? Can you tell us specifically how that came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early May, I was called to the garrison, which is two kilometres to the west in the suburbs. Major Krkljes [phoen] handed me my resignation and he said that this was at my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us in early May. Do you have a specific date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you told us that between the night of the 2nd and the 3rd of May Doboj was taken over by the Serb forces, and you just informed the Trial Chamber that you were basically dismissed. Did this type of dismissal happen to other persons in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was rather widespread. Definitely after the 3rd of May. Except for the work obligation which was introduced in some companies, in certain companies in town. But other than that, everybody who was a non-Serb was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There's one matter I want to deal with in private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Witness, as Judge Harhoff indicated to you, we will be dealing specifically with the issue of the curfew. Just prior to getting to this matter, I would like you to inform the Trial Chamber whether you knew of the creation of a Serb Crisis Staff in the municipality of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that before the war. Later I found out, and it was rather soon, in the early days of the war. And an acquaintance of mine, a military officer, told me on the street that there was a Crisis Staff. He mentioned some people whom I know personally as being members of the Crisis Staff. He said that the Crisis Staff was in charge of everything that was going on, and he had -- commented on why they had handed over authority to the civilians, that is, the Crisis Staff, and he made a link between that and the events that were to ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, sir, could you tell us who is this military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Milovan Stankovic, who, at that time, held the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And had you known Mr. Stankovic for some time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had known him since 1978 or 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he was not a major yet. But it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge what was his role in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point major Stankovic was transferred to Sarajevo where he served in the command of the army. I am not in a position to be more precise as to his position or responsibilities; I don't want to make a mistake. And he came to Doboj in the Autumn of 1991 and he said that he was supposed to help out the garrison commander whose name was Cazim Hadzic. At that time of war, he was commander of the defence of the city. But only for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a few weeks, he was replaced by Colonel Slavko Lisica, who was a commander of the Operations Group and the main commander of the Serb army in that area. And then Stankovic no longer played a role, or at least I'm not aware of any role of his, in either the civilian or the military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, sir, it is an admitted fact in the case that shortly after the takeover a curfew was put in place in the municipality of Doboj. Now, first of all, were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that on the local radio and also directly on the street. There would be vehicles going up and down the streets with large speakers, informing the population that a curfew had been imposed and everything else that had to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When did you first hear of the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately on the 3rd of May in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what were the hours during which this curfew was imposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is easier for me to say when the -- what the hours were without a curfew. We were freely -- free to move from 8.00 till 11.00 a.m., which means three hours out of 24. And we used that time to provide basic supplies such as water. And there was no electricity, so we went out to -- in search of water, food, and so on during these three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that there would be vehicles going up and down the streets with large speakers. What kind of vehicles were these, and to which organisation did they belong to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were both police vehicles and some civilian vehicles that were requisitioned. It is well known that all civilian vehicles were requisitioned there and they were used for various purposes and in various ways. I cannot be precise as to which vehicle circulated on which day. There were smaller military vehicles, armoured personnel carriers, police vehicles. A small bus was used to arrest those who were found on the street and take them to the police. Some people said that they had been fined and then released. Others said that they had been detained and placed in a camp and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Have you witnessed, yourself, such arrests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The building -- from the building where I lived, you had -- had a good view of a piece of land where people cultivated vegetables and fruits. And I saw that on one occasion people who were digging in those small gardens were scooped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "scooped up," who was arresting these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police, local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "the police," do you mean the military or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The military police and the civilian police differed in their clothing and in the vehicles they used. The military police, who were soldiers, wore olive-drab or camouflage uniforms; whereas, the police wore blue uniforms with -- some of them were also of the camouflage type, so-called war uniforms. The police had white belts. What I mean -- and that's the military police. Whereas the civilian police had just regular belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay. And you told us that the local police was arresting people. It is still not clear in your answer which of the two was arresting the people who were not obeying by the curfew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm convinced - and everybody down there knows that - that it was the local civilian police. I have no other technical term. To me, as a soldier, there is the military police and the civilian police on the other hand. And their function should be the protection of the citizens and their property, but that's not what they did, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know, in Doboj, who was the head of the police? The civilian police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know, although I didn't know the man personally. His name was Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the curfew, could you tell the Trial Chamber who did it apply to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, it applied to everybody, according to the -- according to the proclamation. But in practice it only applied to non-Serbs. And I can say with full responsibility, and it was obvious too, that mostly non-Serbs were being taken in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you were saying that it was obvious that mostly non-Serbs were being taken in. Did you see Serbs walking in the streets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them daily. For which reasons, I don't know. Probably because things had to function. I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the Trial Chamber, where -- in which part of Doboj did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the western part of town, near the centre. I had a view of an open area in the direction of the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say that it was near the centre, is there a building of some importance in the vicinity of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near me there was a secondary school, so-called secondary school centre, which was about 150 metres away as the crow flies. And many people were taken there, and from there they were taken to third countries. But that wasn't your question; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to Doboj, we have -- there's a main street. And it is a fact that on this main street there was a court, there was a police station; how far was your apartment from this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 200 to 300 metres to the west. This may not be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Now in relation to the length of the imposition of this curfew, I'd like to ask you exactly how you knew about it. It is admitted in this case that hundreds of Muslims and Croats were detained in Doboj after the takeover. And I would like to ask you, did this occur to you as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't understand what kind of question this is. Is this a direct question or is the Prosecutor putting forward his own position from the Prosecution case so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's just for Your Honours to understand how the witness was able to observe the length of the imposition of the curfew. He may be able to inform you when he was in freedom and when he was not in freedom. So for him to be able to say that to you, he should also be able to say whether he was detained or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see no problem with the question, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then it should simply be put as my learned friend has just said it. Just put a direct question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you detained for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the police station twice but I was released again. Once, I was arrested by the military police and taken to the garrison where I spent a little short of four days and three nights. And owing to some friends and acquaintances, among others - I can give you a name, if necessary; that's not a problem - I was released and could go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I didn't want to get into the details of your detention, sir. It's just for the Trial Chamber to understand you were detained for four days. And could you tell us during which month that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the rest of the year, was there any other period where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was neither detained nor arrested in subsequent periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. After your release, did you notice whether the curfew was still in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, until which part of the year was this curfew in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be very precise, but I believe that it was in place at least until the end of the year. I'm not sure, though, whether the duration of the curfew continued to be 21 hours a day or whether it was changed later, shortened. But there was a curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And until when did you remain in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last day in Doboj was the 25th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned to us earlier about Mr. Stankovic mentioning to you the issue of the Crisis Staff. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, to your knowledge, which authorities imposed this curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke about that with Stankovic, and the reason was our application for help and how we could be assisted, as citizens that were not arrested, that our houses shouldn't be searched. And he said that the authority was -- had been handed over to the civilians, the Crisis Staff, too soon, and that he personally could do very little or nothing to help anybody who was in need of help. I considered, at the time, that the Crisis Staff was an illegal body, because after the multi-party elections, authorities were established; in other words, the assembly, the president. And at other levels, there was a division of power among the parties. But then, suddenly, this body called "Crisis Staff" sprung up, and I knew it was that headed the Crisis Staff. Or at least I know some names; others I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There's one matter you mentioned to the Trial Chamber earlier was in front of your apartment there was this little area where people could plant, I think it was produce or vegetables. How were these being grown? Did they have access to water, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to come back to what the Bench said, that we should not go too far from the topic discussed, and that the topic was the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This very topic is related to the imposition of the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may add that I don't -- I don't think your previous answer [sic] was answered at all. I think the question was: Who was the authority that imposed the curfew. And -- and the question was not answered. But that is -- the precise reason was that it was suggested that it was -- in your question it was -- the Crisis Staff was mentioned. And now the witness has explained us everything about the Crisis Staff except giving us the answer to the question, which is, I believe, relevant to the adjudicated fact. And now we are moving into water-pumps ... I really have -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. It could be dealt in cross-examination, but I'll ask the question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the intervention of the Defence. Could you tell us, if you know, which authority imposed the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who it was specifically. I heard about the curfew, I saw its effects, and I felt it -- felt them. But who sat down and decided to impose it, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: One last question before the break to wrap up on this topic. You told us that you heard about the curfew over the radio. Did the radio announce where did this curfew come from, on whose authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the Crisis Staff who made that decision with the leadership of the police. Because on the radio they said that a curfew was imposed that lasted from, till; and there were people -- or, rather, those vehicles on the streets proclaiming the same thing. But as far as the decision to do that was concerned, I believe the Crisis Staff was mentioned in that context, as well as the police and the chief of police. It is difficult to repeat verbatim that proclamation after so much time. Those were ugly things, and you try to forget them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have about two, three minutes after the break, Your Honours, and I'll be finished with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, before you complete your cross-examination [sic], Mr. Demirdjian, with respect to a matter that was raised by the Prosecution at the beginning of today's sitting, inviting the Chamber to reconsider the Ruling that it gave yesterday with regard to Witness 228, the Chamber is considering it. It isn't in a position, because of the paucity of information, to rule definitively at this point, but it is considering the -- acceding to the request, provided that the witness is available to attend on Monday, the 10th of January, to give evidence in this trial. The consequential decision arising out of that is that the evidence of Brown would be deferred to the week following. But, as I said, that is not a definitive Ruling at this stage; that is the -- where the Chamber is at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And before I continue, may I introduce two new members of the team who have joined us in the courtroom: Mr. Francesco Rindi, who will be taking the next witness; and Ms. Indah Susanti, who will be replacing Mr. Smith next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I have one last question to ask you about the authority over the curfew. You mentioned to us prior to the break - and that's at page 20, line 16 - that Mr. Stankovic had commented on the -- why the authority was handed over to the civilians and that he made a link between that and the events that were to ensue. Can you inform the Trial Chamber, what was that link that he made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand completely what you're asking me. But concerning the relationship between myself and

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). We did not carry out the same type of work, but we met frequently, exchanged information. We understood each other, and we cooperated on certain issues. Now, as to the question how I knew Major Stankovic, and it was contact, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, let me stop you for a second. Just a second, please. Let me make sure you understood my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But before we continue, the witness mentioned at line 8, page 30: "... my work ..." well, I will not say the organisation. If we could redact that part. The organisation in which he was working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. You told us, prior to the break, that Mr. Stankovic spoke to you and he made a comment about handing over the authority to the civilians. And you said: "... that is, the Crisis Staff ..." And you said he made a link between that, the handing over of the authority, and events that were to ensue. And I wanted to ask you: What is that link that he made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. Concerning the safety of citizens of the town and the persecution and the harassment that they suffered, the looting, and all these others, negative phenomena, that were happening there, he told me that in that context that they had handed over authority to the civilians too early. By "them," he meant the army. And that in that respect he was helpless in terms of being able to act to provide the protection to those who needed it, and, that is, the civilians. I know that he himself tried to provide help on -- in many individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And when you said that "he meant the army," did he tell you, in terms of the authority to the civilians, who specifically this was handed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume, judging from this conversation, that that referred to the military authority that was transferred to the so-called civilian sector, that is to say, the Crisis Staff, the civilian police, and other civilian authorities that were functioning at the time in the territory where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. The last topic I want to go back to is the issue of the water-pump that was across from your apartment, sir. Did people go get water between the hours that you told us, between 8.00 a.m. and 11.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only pump in the neighbourhood where I lived which supplied water. Before that, it had been used by people who were involved in gardening, for watering the plants and sowing and seedlings; however, during the war we used it exclusively for drinking water but also for other needs of the population, such as hygiene and things of that nature. At one point in time, the police banned the usage of this water regardless of the time-period allowed for movement, which was three hours a day, between 8.00 and 11.00 in the morning. So during that period we were prohibited from taking water from that pump. It was even locked with some chains or things like that, and we were driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you specifically. You were saying irrespective of the time. Did you see anybody being arrested during the hours of 8.00 a.m. and 11.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any arrests, especially since movement was virtually limited at any time, and it was dangerous. I wouldn't like to discuss this issue. For example, I sustained some injuries, but I thought it was better to try and -- and cope with that, rather than venture out and expose one's self to danger. But as I said, I didn't see any arrests outside my flat expect for the occasion which I mentioned in my previous statement when a bus that was used to arrest people who were found on the street or close to streets, at -- in any public place whatsoever, during the curfew those people would be arrested and driven away, I suppose, to the police. Some of them returned, saying that they were released after having paid a fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And one last question on this topic. Do you know of anyone who was specifically arrested? Do you know specifically someone who was arrested for violating the curfew? Do you have examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it refers to the people who were doing the gardening which is next to the street. And that is when this bus and the police came and arrested those people and took them away. I remember a sort of a paradox. A man called Radovan - and judging by his name we assumed he was a Serb, and we were surprised that he was arrested, being a Serb. Eventually we found out that he was a Croat, that he was originally from Herzegovina, and that there they have names that resemble those of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Before I conclude, if you could just tell the Trial Chamber, you told us you left in October 1993, could you just tell us why you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left, first and foremost, for the sake of my own safety and the safety of my family. Starting from the beginning of May 1992 until the 25th of October, 1993, non-Serbs were leaving on a daily basis. They were collected in front of the so-called secondary school centre and then were transported by buses from there. I heard that they crossed via Gradiska to Croatia and then onwards to third countries. The fact is that nowadays the people are scattered all over the place from Australia, where my sister lives, to Holland where I lived. The fact is that out of my six siblings only one of them still lives down there. And believe me, there are thousands of families like that, and I would just call it ethnic cleansing. I don't know how else to call it because -- I can't say that it has been accomplished 100 per cent, but let's say 90 per cent. And I don't think that any return and normalisation of the situation is possible. I do apologise. I hope that was the question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I put a few questions to this witness, can we move to private session for a moment, please? Or a closed session, as suggested by my learned friend Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why closed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, private will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, immediately after the occupation of the town, the Serbian municipality of Doboj was established, and Drago Ljubicic was appointed president. The president of the Executive Committee was Borislav Paravac; and Major Stankovic, Milovan Stankovic, was appointed defence commander of the town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The previously-formed Crisis Staff declared a state of war, imposed curfew, ordered mobilisation of the entire Serbian population, and appointed commissioners for all the companies and institutions of authority in the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So you will, therefore, agree with me that there was no dilemma whatsoever; that it was the Crisis Staff who imposed the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were the highest-ranking organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was the highest organ in a socio-political community that organised life at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I asked you to finish this because you obviously anticipated my next question. Very well. Now I'm going to show you now Exhibit 1D260.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to take a look at this document before I ask a question, and it is related to what we discussed a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. But, of course, I have never had this document in my hands, and I don't see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I assumed as much, but you can see that it was exactly the Crisis Staff who prescribed measures relating to the violation of the curfew, that the -- banned any public gatherings, and that certain punishments and -- were envisaged. You can see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to ask you about that. Yes, that is what I wanted to ask you exactly with relations to your previous answer. Do you agree that the Crisis Staff was the main organ in charge of the functioning of the municipality in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Could Mr. Cvijetic let us know where in this document the curfew is mentioned. I tried to glance at it very quickly, and I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under item 1 it is said that movement is being restricted and that no people should be outside during curfew, and there's reference to the Crisis Staff decision. So the curfew is mentioned under item 1, and we have the testimony of this witness to the effect that it was the Crisis Staff who imposed the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I don't see the word "curfew." I don't see the imposition or any timings. There's an issue of moving and loitering in the streets. No specific time. And it doesn't really mention the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I'm sorry. I agree. But let's clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, there is mention here specifically the time that you spoke about, so moving or staying in the streets is banned other than during the period allowed for procuring supplies. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One can see that this decision was taken by the Serbian municipality of Doboj in accordance with the rules of public law and order which allows for certain bans to be imposed. I still claim that the movement was restricted throughout the day, except during the period from 8.00 until 11.00 in the morning. I don't see who signed this, but this is irrelevant to me, because I personally felt the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. But in item 1 it is said that anyone found on the streets outside that time-period, which is allowed for provisions to be obtained, would be punishable. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, there's no relevance in this document to a time-period. There's no reference - sorry - to a time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether, Mr. Cvijetic, there is a companion document that this is cross referenced with that you would wish to ... for whatever purposes you're showing this to the witness. Because in terms of the question you've asked so far, Article 1.1 speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I showed him this document as part of his testimony and his claim that the main organ which took care of the functioning of life in Doboj municipality was the Crisis Staff. Furthermore, his claim that the Crisis Staff prescribed the curfew, introduced mobilisation, was the basis; and we see from the heading that the Crisis Staff also envisaged punishment for moving outside of the time designated for shopping. That was his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, I think you -- I think you've missed the point that Mr. Demirdjian made and which -- which, as we understand it, is that this document, particularly Article 1.1 to which you are referring the witness, is all well and good in itself but on the face of it, it doesn't say anything about the times of a curfew. And therein lies the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The second thing, Your Honour, in terms of how the evidence is being referred to, Mr. Cvijetic is saying that: "Furthermore, his claim that the Crisis Staff prescribed the curfew." During his evidence in-chief, he involved the Crisis Staff and the police. So in terms of misstating the evidence, I think we should be careful about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the witness a clear question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, item 1, which you see, and you can read what is says, does it relate to what you testified about? Does it relate to the time which was meant for shopping and the time which wasn't meant for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain that this document talks about the introduction of the curfew in the field. This document, which has the principles in it, it is the highest organ that designates how one should carry itself in such circumstances. However, it doesn't list the time to which the ban applies; it just says that fines will be imposed. Now who applied this decision, I believe, should be the person who should be asked. Somebody elaborated on this, and I believe it would be logical that the chief of police would adhere to this, that the commander of town would adhere to this, and that other important organs would participate in implementing this decision by the highest socio-political organ in a certain community, or in a certain territory. That's my answer. I can't tell you exactly what the author meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you allow. Mr. Witness, one simple question. You told us you heard about a curfew on the radio. Is this what is said under 1? Is what you heard on the radio? Under point 1 of Article 1. Is that what you heard on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. Not verbatim. The radio read out orders, read out messages on their loud-speakers. They talked about movement, they talked to loitering, they talked about bans and fines; and this is something general. Now what we had was something more specific - naming the time, from and to. Movement after 11.00 in the morning and movement before 8.00 in the morning, that is to say, movement was allowed for a total of three hours, between 8.00 and 11.00. I can draw my own conclusion based on this. In my opinion, this is just a draft that was made by somebody to have order in town. As for who implemented this and based on whose further decisions, I really don't know. It is logical that the police and the army would be involved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. Now that you've mentioned the army, would you agree with me conclusion that in that period, or in a part of that period, the town was under military administration, practically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Serbian army entered town in the night between the 2nd and the 3rd and until a week or two - I'm not certain - later, the military administration functioned on its own rules. I didn't know until when they functioned and when the so-called civilian organs took over power. I found out about that, and I explained that in my earlier testimony how. It was by accident that I heard of this from Mr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You said that Major Stankovic was replaced by Colonel Lisica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know about some measures that he, as commander, took and certain limitations or restrictions that he imposed as town commander and as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not specifically. I wasn't in such a position. But I know that on the radio he declared that the Serbian People were poorer than other people. He had inflammatory statements; said that people had the right to take things from other people's houses. And my interpretation was - and I apologise to you and the Prosecution and the Court - I interpreted this as an invitation to looting, because there was state of war. And I apologise to the Court for moving on. Despite this, there was no war in Doboj. Proof of that is the last issue of the local paper which was then called "Glas Komune," and the title was: Doboj Liberated Without a Single Bullet Fired. So I was shocked --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll ask you specifically about this. Do you know that Colonel Lisica mobilized people in the territory of Doboj municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know that he even mobilized the civilian police and dispatched the chief of police to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But I know that based on the system of subordination, in a certain territory where there's combat, or where combat is expected, as a principle, and based on the law, the civilian police is resubordinated to a higher military command. I believe that's how things are in all countries. As for the mobilisation, I saw how it was done in the JNA centre and at the garrison when I was detained. Now whether he ordered or somebody else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. You again anticipated one of my questions. Since you were doing the work that you were doing, you know about this very well. Now, tell me, was Doboj shelled throughout that time, or a part of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not initially. It happened in the middle of the year that a shell or two would fall. For a while we were surprised that shells arrived from the west, that is, from the north-west, and we were certain that this was not a shell from the enemy territory but an own shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll ask you specifically --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How many victims were there as a result of this shelling in Doboj? Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were casualties, but I don't know the number. It wasn't a large number; I know that for a fact, because, as a rule, there was always an alert given to the civilians. It was a caricature, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you could just answer my specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would go down to the basement and shelling would start but by the other side. To be specific, in my own neighbourhood I saw two or three shells land. One landed in front of my entrance and it broke a window. Nobody was hurt. And another shell landed in a yard and again nobody hurt. And I know that one shell landed near the SUP, and I believe somebody was injured there. A man who was on his way back from hospital got hit. It was quite a memorable situation; that's why I remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was a memorial raised to the victims of this shelling? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a memorial in front of the SUP building in Doboj, but I think that this is a memorial to fallen policemen, primarily policemen, at the front, who were killed at the front where there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a memorial in Doboj. Actually there are two: one from the First World War and the second one from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you don't know it, I'll just move on. Furthermore, you talked about a shortage of electricity. This power cut, did it relate to the entire municipality? Was everybody out of power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'll put a claim to you which largely relies upon your own testimony. The curfew, as was prescribed, related to all civilians in Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: During the curfew - and I'm asking whether you know - people who worked in certain services which had to function were able to move, but they had to have a licence; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in that position myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So you had a permit to move during the curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Because you had to go to work and you had to go home. And you had to take the shortest route.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that by accident, because we have testimony from others that other non-Serbs who worked in specific services had such permits and were allowed to move around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not a Serb. I told you what I was. And I was under work obligation in the (redacted). I had a decision and I had an approval from the responsible organ of the Secretariat for National Defence and from the president of the court saying that I was able to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was it the case with other services and with other employees who worked in these services who had to go to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody had a decision where I worked. And where I worked, the registrar of the court issues these -- issued these permits. As for other places, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it still the position that there are no questions from ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We don't have a question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir -- if we could have that document back on the screen that Mr. Cvijetic showed you, 1D260, exhibit. Exhibit 1D260. Is it still there? Okay. Can you see the date on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's this document, then the date is 28 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. At page 21 today, earlier, you answered one of my questions and you said that you heard the curfew -- you heard of the curfew immediately on the 3rd of May, 1992. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, in relation to the curfew which this document does not specifically deal with, Mr. Cvijetic put to you that the Crisis Staff issued the decision relating to the curfew. Can you remind us, who saw to it that it was enforced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my answer to Defence counsel, I said that based on this document I can't say that it says Crisis Staff, and I can't see a signature. Therefore, this bare document tells me of general measures passed by somebody. But the curfew was being enforced by the police. Some kind of an agricultural commune can't be enforcing the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, at page 42 just now, Mr. Cvijetic put to you that Doboj was under "military administration." Could you tell the Trial Chamber which forces were regulating the life in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the 2nd and 3rd of May, as day broke, I saw - and a colleague of mine visited me at home, we had been colleagues until then - the army, which they called the Serbian army, had white lilies on a red surface which they wore. And that was when I found out that the Serbian army had taken control of town, and I found out that Stankovic was the town commander, and so on. And everything that happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about the subordination of the police to the army and you said that when combat was expected, the police was subordinated to the army. And then Mr. Cvijetic asked you whether you knew that the chief of police was mobilised. Now, do you know anything about the relationship between the chief of the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave the only answer I could, both to you and to him. As I'm aware of the regulations as they were before the war, the police was always subordinated to a higher military command in the territory where certain combat is happening. Now, whether that was what happened in this specific case, I don't know. I don't know that. I also don't know whether the chief was mobilized. I know that he became chief before the war. And before him, another man had been chief, who was replaced right at the very beginning of the war. And we commented by saying that he was not good enough for the new authorities and for the new regime that had power and that that was the reason that he was replaced. Whether he was mobilized, whether he was one the carrying out the mobilisation, whether he was implementing this decision that the Defence talked about, or to what extent, I just know that the curfew was in place from, until, and I know what practice was. And practice was not what it says here. I personally would have signed this, in the situation that was. But, in practice, in wartime, things are not implemented that way; otherwise there wouldn't have been persecutions, arrests, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that the chief of police was quickly replaced. Who is this man you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I referred to the chief of police who was chief before the war, before the 3rd of May, 1992. He was replaced by one Andrija Bjelosevic, a man I don't know. I don't even think that he hails from the town in which I was born and where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You were also asked about shelling and casualties. Now, how many shells in total fell on the town of Doboj during your time there? To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that was a short question and my answer will be even shorter. I can't really reflect the situation as it was. If I say that there were ten shells, it will be wrong. If I say 50, it will be wrong again. A number of shells did fall while I was there, but I didn't count them. When there was an attack, the children counted the shells. But Doboj wasn't shelled daily; and when it was shelled, it wasn't shelled massively. When the first shell fell somewhere, we would hear it or see it, and then we said, Wait till the third one falls and after the third one there will be no more, then you can move freely about. And you can believe me that's how it was. It is true that Doboj is not a devastated city. It is well preserved. True it is somewhat poorer than it was, but to a larger extent it is preserved. There have been shells, but I haven't counted them so I cannot give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Could you tell us, in which part of the year did the -- did most of these shells fall? You were there during 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of 1993, there were more shells, somewhat more. And now I remember a case. I saw from my balcony when I was looking toward the garrison there was a tanker truck passing by and I know that it was hit on that road. But, generally speaking, in the spring and summer of 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"], there was more shelling. Actually, it was more returning fire. Don't misunderstand me. More than in 1992, when it was really, very rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And the last topic that you were asked about was about the laissez-passer that you were given by the authorities. First of all, in -- you said you worked (redacted). How many other non-Serbs were working there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how many non-Serbs were awarded such passes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I worked, there were only Serbs and me. And I'm not -- I'm not a Serb. So they couldn't get any laissez-passers or any documents. I got one. I was a local. People knew me --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and they chose me for reasons known to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: My question was: Generally speaking, in the town of Doboj, do you know how passes were given to non-Serbs, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness answered. When asked by me, he said he couldn't answer. I asked him the same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there was a work obligation --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's let the witness finish, because he was answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: As for other institutions and firms, I don't know whether they got laissez-passers; that's what you asked about. But I know that they went there to work, because they were under work obligation. And people went to work to the timber-processing plant, to the food-processing plant, to the machinery plant, but they went there in an organised fashion. Whether or not they had laissez-passers is something about which I can only speculate, and I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to clarify the matter. You're saying that people were going these various places; my question specifically refers to non-Serbs. Were these people, (redacted) (redacted) were these people non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were ordered to go there. Ordered by the authorities. Because the manufacturing process had to be kept up, work had to continue. And after a short while they were also expelled from the territory like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And one last question on this issue, sir. When were you given this laissez-passer? Which part of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I have to calculate. I left Doboj on the 25th of October, and I had worked for 11 months, which means that it would have been Autumn 1992. It may have been early October or late December, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps you can explain to the Judges how it is that you got this laissez-passer, who gave you this laissez-passer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home, as usual, because movement was prohibited. We couldn't visit neighbours. We couldn't assemble for any reason. And they came for me, that is, the then-commander's driver came, and the commander was Stankovic at the time, and he took me to the JNA centre, which was about 150 to 200 metres from my house. There he introduced me to two other men and said, We'll have you work here with this man. That's what they had decided. Who exactly, I don't know. But I think that it was Stankovic who had personally helped me to perform my work obligation there. What had I done to deserve that? It may sound absurd, but nothing. But it was important to me that in this way I may have been better protected than those who had no documents at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I noticed that at page 50, line 23, I mentioned the location where the witness worked. Being the only non-Serb there, he might be easily identified. If we could redact that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, at -- sorry. I have one clarification for the transcript as well. At page 50, line 18, the witness said: "... generally speaking, in the spring and summer" and here it reads "of 1992, there was more shelling." I think that we heard something else. Sir, could you clarify that for us, if the year is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said 1993. I may have misspoken, in which case I apologise. But it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Cvijetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another correction to the transcript. It's, again, about a date. Page 52, line 14, reads that -- to the Prosecutor's question when he got the pass allowing him to move about, we see December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But I believe you said something else. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I left on the 25th of October, 1993. That's when I left Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just say when you got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I went 11 months back, which then would be this latter half of September or early October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's when I received the decision that I had -- was under work obligation and I got a workplace --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, you've already said as much. It was just the date that mattered to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's just on the time that we take the break, so we'd rise now and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before -- or, Mr. Demirdjian, before we rise, this is perhaps something you should take care of during the break. We are reminded that Ms. Pidwell said this morning about -- it's about ST-228. Ms. Pidwell said this morning that ST-228 should, for a reason that we don't know of, testify first in Karadzic. Then she said there would then have to be a day's break, at least, while his transcript was considered by the Defence. So that would mean -- if this is correct, that would mean that he couldn't testify in this case on Monday. And that would mean also that if he could -- if he would testify on -- in Karadzic on Monday and then leave one day in between, we would be on the -- on the Wednesday afternoon. We have more or less two sessions on the Wednesday afternoon. That wouldn't be enough. There is a real problem there. But we don't see why -- why it would be necessary to have him in Karadzic first. And we would insist, if we would consider the -- the OTP's application to have him in the first week of January, to have him on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will -- I don't know the precise answer to that. I will check, Your Honour, and get back to you. I know that was the proposal, to have him testify in Karadzic on Monday and testify in this case on Wednesday. Mr. Brown to start on Monday the 17th. And maybe one or two other witnesses somewhere in there depending on your decision on another pending application. But I will check and try to report back to you before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have to realize -- OTP has to realize that having this witness on Wednesday, there would probably be a problem and he would have to stay over for the -- until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will advise her and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because on Wednesday we would be unable to start until 3.00. So there would only be a little more than two sessions left for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And we don't sit on the Thursday and Friday, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, of course, the other aspect of this is that if the sequence on which the OTP insists, as in the passage read out by Judge Delvoie, how -- what -- how certain can you be in your representations - and I say "you"; not you personally but the OTP in its representations - to this Chamber of that witness coming in Karadzic on the Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours. And maybe the simplest solution is: We have him first and Karadzic follows us. That's something I'll discuss and get back to you about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, is the witness released?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Bench has some questions of the witness, after which we have a short oral ruling to deliver, then we will hear from counsel as to whether they have a report on the matter we raised just before the break. And we will take the adjournment for the day, because it is obvious that we couldn't complete the next witness before, so we would begin his testimony tomorrow. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, about the laissez-passer you got. I understand you got that somewhere in the Autumn of 1992, which means, first of all, that you were under the curfew obligation from May to Autumn 1992; that's right? Without the laissez-passer. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. But I was obliged to respect it even later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Now, that's my -- my second question. While under curfew on the one hand but with a laissez-passer for your work obligation -- I should first have confirmed that your work obligation was something that had nothing to do with your previous functions from which you were dismissed. That was what -- what was called in the -- in the region "work obligation," and that could be anything; right? I don't -- I don't need any other specification. Okay. Now, this laissez-passer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This laissez-passer, did that -- did it allow you to move around freely within -- within the hours that you normally could not without laissez-passer, or was it only -- did it only permit you to go to work and come back and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understood that to mean that I could go to work and come back home; no more than that. Which means from 7.00 a.m. till 3.00 p.m. I could go to work without obstacles and go back from work. That's how I understood it, and that's how I behaved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now something else. You told us you lived at -- well, practically in the centre of Doboj. Was that a -- where you live, was that a mixed neighbourhood, with people of mixed ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, then, during the curfew, let's say before the Autumn of 1992, to keep it simple, as from 11.00 in the morning you were in your apartment and you couldn't move; right? You could -- you could see what happened in the street because you had -- you could see that; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you -- did you see -- move people around while you were inside and could not go out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, very few people moved about. And I knew many people because -- and many people knew me because I was born and raised there; however, I said [as interpreted] many unknown persons in civilian clothes and also in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to, let's say, normal people from your neighbourhood. You had -- you had Serb neighbours? I don't ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that -- and I said as much in my statement, that the curfew was mostly honoured by non-Serbs. There were cases of neighbours who declared that they were Serbs and who could move about freely and return, but the others were not allowed to go out and -- on the street, if they were not Serbs. I can claim that with full responsibility. In my building, there were 18 apartments. Out of these 18, ten or 11 families were non-Serbs. And they were all in their apartments. Some had to leave their apartments earlier, some later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm more interested in the people that did not stay in their apartment during the curfew. So the -- the -- the other -- you said ten families were -- were of Muslim ethnicity and the others were of Serb ethnicity, I suppose; did they go out freely? Did you see -- did you see them go out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, most Serbs who were healthy and of age had already been engaged by the police, the military, or by the firms where they worked. Or -- their families, children, wives, if the wives were not employed, freely moved about in their neighbourhood, stayed outside, played. Even my girl, who was four at the time, played with them during the time when there was no curfew. So they could move about, but the others could not. Believe me. I don't know -- I don't know what else I can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I have three questions for you. And the first question is, actually, a question that will follow up on the questions just put to you by Judge Delvoie. Because, Mr. Witness, it is still not quite clear - to me at least - just how this matter of the curfew was organised. You are saying that it was discriminatory in the sense that although it applied to everyone, formally speaking, it was practiced in such a manner as to allow Serbs to move around freely during all hours of the day, while non-Serbs were ordered to stay inside after 11.00 in the morning, and, if they were seen on the streets after 11.00 and before 8.00 next morning, they would be arrested. You also told us that the people who had to go to work in order to maintain vital functions of the town, that is to say, the -- the factories that you mentioned earlier on, that for all the workers there, they would be given laissez-passers which would allow them, actually, to go to work and come back again, and that in those instances many laissez-passers were given to non-Serbs. Can I ask you if this is correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said of myself for -- that I had received one; whereas the others who were under work obligation, I can't say that they received any. But it's a fact that they went to do their work obligation. I can give you an example. When I tried to check how my mother was doing, who was living two kilometres to the south of the centre of town, and that was during the time when movement was allowed, I was stopped at the police check-point, and my wife, who accompanied me, was told that I shouldn't go down that way again because I would be arrested. And I never tried to do so again, neither during the time of free movement nor during the curfew. I only received the approval to go to work and come back. We were, literally speaking, in house arrest. Whether the other employees got passes, I cannot say. Now I remember a detail though. In front of the police building in the centre of town, there was a small kiosk, and a policeman was sitting there who would give permission to somebody who had some business to do, such as go to pharmacy to get some medication, which was only a few hundred metres away. He would get a special card with his personal information, and with that card he would then -- that person would go there, do what he had to do fast, and return soon. And as for all the other people who were in town, who regulated their affairs, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And this policeman who would give the special permissions that you just mentioned, would that be required even in the open hours, between 8.00 and 11.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My father-in-law had to go to his weekend cottage, which was a few hundred metres away, to take something from that cottage, some books, books that were -- or something, and he got such a permission for -- or, rather, to go there during the time when there -- when you could move about freely. They called it prevention. At that moment, nobody could know for sure whether this or that house was mine or somebody else's. So then even during those hours when movement was free, you needed permission to go to a certain place. And there were controls in place, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for -- for drilling into this, but it is important for the Chamber to understand how things worked in practice, so I'll -- let me put a few more questions to you in relation to this issue about the curfew. Suppose, sir, that you were in your apartment and it would be 9.00 in the morning and you wanted to go down and get yourself a pack of cigarettes; would that be possible? Could you just walk out of your apartment, go down the stairs, enter into the street, and walk over to whatever the tobacco shop was and get yourself your pack of cigarettes, and then walk back without being stopped? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in principle. On one occasion, I did exactly as you described, only I wanted to buy some fresh meat that I had heard arrived in the nearby butchers, and I bought some meat. At that very moment, two police entered the shop, because the police station was just opposite it, and I heard them saying, Look at this man -- [microphone not activated]. There are more of them. And I learned a lesson from them, and I immediately went home. I was security-conscious at the time, and therefore I tried to stay indoors as much as possible.
