For example, when my daughter got ill, I had to see a doctor who was also dismissed from work, although he was a Serb. But I asked him to come over to a house visit to examine her and give her injections. But these are the moments when you have to take risks, otherwise it was undesirable. In addition to the police, there were some other formations who belonged, I don't know to whom. I, as a soldier, could not understand that such formations could exist, because a person holding a certain position carries certain responsibility for that, so I expected this to be at least respected in terms of how it was written. However, the daily practice in Bosnia-Herzegovina was something else. And later I heard that this same practice prevailed in the majority of places and towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So, if I understand you correctly, the -- during the times of the curfew, the difference between Serbs and non-Serbs was really that, while, on the one hand, the non-Serbs chose to stay indoors as much as possible, even in the so-called open hours; while the Serbs simply disregarded it. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I assert. However, during the time outside curfew hours, all the chores and businesses were done by women and mainly elderly women at that. Men had to behave differently. They were expected to keep a low profile. That is why women tried to use these three hours to do their shopping and other chores that were necessary for keeping their households. And I call this discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that was -- when we looked at this decision, this is something that didn't happen in reality. In practice, it was completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly: If -- my summary of your testimony here is that Serb men and women did not feel that they were obliged to respect the curfew in Doboj in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So Serb men and women would leave their houses and go out into the public areas regardless of the curfew, and if they were stopped by a police and checked who they were, then they would be allowed to move on, rather than being arrested. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Most of them knew each other, and they went about even without any checking. We sometimes said that we should try and stick our ID cards on our foreheads. It's not a nice thing to say, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And your testimony is also that Serbs could move around freely, irrespective of whether they had special laissez-passers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I stand by my statement that they moved freely, regardless of any restrictions or curfews. But that applies at least to my neighbourhood. There are friends of mine, there are neighbours of mine, but apparently these restrictions did not apply to everyone, and that is why I felt discriminated against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Let me move to the second question, which relates to the two times that you were arrested yourself. And my question is just this: Were you arrested during the curfew hours, or were you arrested in the open hours, between 8.00 and 11.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested during the period when we were free to move. And this is what happened: I wanted to check on my mother, who lived two kilometres south of Doboj. At the exit point of the town, a patrol appeared. First they beat me, then they put me on a lorry and drove me to the police station. There was an inspector there who received me. He knew me from before. And after a brief conversation, he let me go home. I only asked him to escort me out of the building because there was a so-called gauntlet of police officers, because whenever somebody was brought in, they would just kick them or punch them, and in order to avoid that I asked him to escort him -- to escort me out, and he did. He was a Serb, but he was a good friend of mine. But the fact remains that this incident happened during the hours outside the curfew, when there were open hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. My third and last question relates to something that you said at the very beginning of your testimony this morning; namely, the order that came from what you called the superior command to collect all the weapons from the TOs and hand those weapons over to the JNA. And you said that this took place in the fall of 1991. And my question to you is this: Do you know who issued those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This order was issued by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in Belgrade through the highest command of the Territorial Defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was called the Republican Headquarters or Staff of the TO. The approval for that was given by the then-Presidency, or, rather, the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, we are talking about a decision that is interlinked, and it was implemented 100 per cent in our territory. I have some information that elsewhere that wasn't the case, but in our territory it was implemented 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, sir. I have no further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank you, sir, for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be excused. Mr. Hannis will remain in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian. The -- we are delivering this oral ruling at this stage. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion of 5th November, 2010, requesting that the Chamber review its order of 17th of September wherein it held that: "There is an overriding public interest" in General Manojlo Milovanovic's evidence being presented orally. In the motion, the Prosecution requests that the evidence of this witness be presented pursuant to Rule 92 bis. In addition, the Prosecution requests to add one of its investigators, Mr. Blaszczyk, ST-262, to its witness list as a Rule 92 ter witness. Dealing firstly with the Prosecution's investigator. The Chamber concludes that this witness should not be added to the Prosecution's witness list. The witness is not relevant, as he is unable to testify to the core issue of the matter, that is, the authenticity of the Mladic notebooks. The Chamber notes that he cannot testify to the whole chain of custody. Moreover, the Chamber recalls, having held on 17th of September, that the testimony of another Prosecution investigator concerning the chain of custody of the notebooks was unnecessary to establish the prima facie authenticity of the notebooks. The Chamber does not see any reason to reconsider this opinion in respect of further chain of custody evidence in view of the available evidence of General Milovanovic who the Chamber considers to be able to provide the best evidence regarding the notebook's authenticity. It will, therefore, deny the motion in respect of ST-262. In respect of General Milovanovic, the Chamber held on the 17th of September that the witness's statement, wherein it is stated that he had reviewed all the notebooks, was sufficient to establish prima facie authenticity of the notebooks. However, in view of the nature of the witness's anticipated evidence, the Chamber concluded that there is an overriding public interest in its being presented orally. Nevertheless, the Chamber stated that it would consider reviewing the situation if "by the time that the witness is due to be called, similar evidence has already been provided to the Tribunal orally and in public in other proceedings." Having now considered General Milovanovic's testimony in the Stanisic and Simatovic case, which, by decision of the 23rd of November of the Trial Chamber hearing that case was made public, the Chamber is persuaded that the witness is able to offer evidence on the authenticity of the notebooks as required by Rule 89(C). There is a live challenge by the Defence both to the authenticity and the contents of the notebooks insofar as they relate to the events charged by the Prosecution in this case. The Chamber recalls holding on the 17th of September that the addition of this witness will "protect the rights of the accused by providing the Defence an opportunity to challenge the authenticity of the notebooks." Therefore, General Milovanovic will be able to provide the Chamber with the best evidence regarding the notebooks' authenticity. Given the importance of the matter to the present proceedings, the fact that there is no other available witness who may testify to the authenticity of the notebooks and the Defence's live challenge, the Chamber rules that General Milovanovic shall be called viva voce. General Milovanovic shall testify in the -- as to the authenticity of the notebooks and - but only to the extent that he has first-hand knowledge of entries therein that pertain to the time-period relevant to the present case - the contents of the notebooks. The Trial Chamber orders the Prosecution to call General Milovanovic before the winter recess and allows three hours for the examination-in-chief. The Defence is ordered to inform the Chamber of how much time it would request for the cross-examination of this witness. Before we adjourn, do -- does the OTP have a further report on the matter that the Chamber raised before the last break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I did speak with Ms. Pidwell, and we can make some arrangements concerning Witness ST-228 that I think will address the Trial Chamber's concerns. But she requests that you not direct us not to have him testify on a particular day. That matter we wish to leave in our hands until we have a decision from you about a couple of other pending matters for other witnesses. I think ST-263 and 264 are witnesses that we're seeking to add. That may affect the scheduling, and we need to consider all those at the same time. And your discussion at the earliest possible date will be helpful because we anticipate we may need to request summons for those witnesses, or subpoenas for those witnesses. And given the holidays, we would need to process those earlier rather than later to assure that those witnesses attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, in respect of Witness 228, the way I understand this problem is that if the Prosecution wants to hear him in the first week after the recess, that is to say, in the week of Monday, the 10th of January, 2011, then the only day on which he can testify would be on Monday, the 10th. And the issue that relates to the other witnesses that you mentioned, they would have to be called the following week, in any case. And I'm not hereby giving any position on whether or not we will allow those witnesses to appear at all, but even if they were to come, they would not -- they would only be called for the following week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand there's a possibility that ST-228 could, for -- hypothetically speaking, appear on Tuesday the 11th. And we have two sessions on the 12th, as I understand it. We have Monday, Tuesday, and two sessions on Wednesday. So there's a possibility that if you grant the pending application for one or more of the other witnesses, that other witness might be better suited to appear on Monday, and ST-228 on Tuesday. I'm only speaking hypothetically. I don't know all the circumstances. But this is what I've gleaned from speaking with Ms. Pidwell ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So in respect of 228, the -- the choice is that if he is to come, then he shall appear here either Monday or Tuesday, the 10th or the 11th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So our goal is to finish with ST-228 during the week of the 10th, 11th, and 12th. Our other goal is to finish all witnesses that we have left at that time by the end of the following week, January 17th to the 21st.
